claims.text: The onset and progression of melting in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by heterogeneous melting initiated at surface defect sites.
Surface defects lower the local melting point by enhancing atomic diffusion and configurational entropy.
Localized melting propagates gradually from the nanoparticle surface toward its core.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and single phase.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles possess inherent surface defects.
Chemical surface passivation reduces the surface-defect density relative to as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Surface defects and disorder locally reduce cohesive strength and increase atomic mobility.
Increased atomic mobility at surface defects produces an earlier local configurational-entropy increase that overcomes local bonding.
Defect-rich nanoparticles will begin melting at a lower temperature than passivated nanoparticles.
Defect-rich nanoparticles will exhibit a gradual surface-to-core phase transition.
Passivated nanoparticles will have a delayed melting onset relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the heating experiment.
Surface effects dominate the thermal response of nanoparticles in the single-digit to tens-of-nanometers size range.
Controlled heating rates minimize bulk-diffusion effects.
In situ electron microscopy and diffraction can be used to track thermally induced nanoparticle structural or phase evolution.
Equivalent melting onset and progression in passivated and native particles would falsify the proposed surface-defect control mechanism.
The quantitative shift in melting-onset temperature is not specified.
The relative contributions of atomic diffusion and configurational entropy remain unresolved.
